To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ROCs for item and source recognition can both be fit by a single model that assumes that the decision process for both tasks is the same, that the decision process is a detection-theoretically defined process of comparing the strength of the test item to the relative strengths of alternative sources, and that the decision process does not include a recollection component.

(1) the ROCs for item and source recognition are quite different, suggesting that they are based on quite different decision processes; (2) these differences can be accounted for by assuming a detection-theoretically defined decision space and a model of decision-making that is based only on the relative strength of the two sources and the item strength; and (3) the model can account for the ROCs of three canonical data sets, and the ROCs for one data set are given in the text,

a single decision model can account for both source and item recognition, that the decision space is defined by item strength and source strengths, and that the model can account for the data without assuming recollection-specific processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a complete decision model to account for recognition memory data.
the development of a model that accounts for the full range of data from recognition memory experiments.
the development of a complete decision model for item and source recognition that can account for the entire data set without recourse to processes specific to source memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single, simple decision process can account for the entire range of recognition data.
a complete decision model for source and item recognition is still under construction.
the data are not inconsistent with a model that assumes a single detection space and that does not invoke recollection-specific processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the data are best described as a single decision process, but that the nature of the decision process is different from that previously proposed.
the ROCs of source and item memory tasks can be explained by the same model, but that source memory is more sensitive than item memory.
source recognition, item recognition, and confidence are all based on the same decision process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a model of source recognition need not be more complicated than one of item recognition.
a single decision model can account for both source and item recognition, and that this account does not require recollection.
the ROCs of item and source tests can be fit by the same model, suggesting that they are generated by the same underlying processes.
